title: Draft: Proto: Implement new timescales
description:
Added Universal Time 1 (UT1), International Atomic Time (TAI),
Terrestrial Time (TT), GPS Time (GPST), Galileo System Time (GST) and
BeiDou Time (BDT) timescales, for UT1 and TAI also with NTP variant
with all-zero-handling.

These new timescales are internally based on UNIX timestamps which
represent strict 86400 SI seconds per day. Timestamps include leap
seconds, which means that a timestamp pauses, repeates or jumps when
leap seconds are added or deleted. They are not 'visible' in the
timestamp.

The new timescales are continous timescales which means its value
constantly increases over time and is not corrected by leap seconds.

When using the timescales, it is important to know the current offset
to UTC to generate appropriate UNIX timestamps. In other use-cases
(like NTPv5 TAI) the initial offset to UTC and leap seconds are already
included in the on-wire timestamp.

The ISO 8601 representation is extended by `{ts}` scientific extensions.
This is probably the normative ISO 8601-2:2019/Amd 1:2025 notation
for this purpose.

dfilter makes use of this notation, but as it internally matches UNIX
timestamps, the timescale does not have an effect on the actual match.

Ping !25810

added 1 commit
  • 5cdb14b3 - Proto: Implement new timescales
[Compare with previous version](/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/25913/diffs?diff_id=1923726817&start_sha=0eb3379b5c2a42c779832eb82cf0ef2ae8271da9)

The `ABSOLUTE_TIME_` values are for the format when *outputting/displaying* time. (The NTP special handling when zero could possibly be replaced with the newly introduced time_value_string.) Do we need to output all these timescales, as opposed to reading times which are encoded in various timescales (and possibly, if desired, not translate time information to UTC before storing in a nstime_t but instead store in nstime_t information about the time scale - that would make various operations possibly a bit more difficult.)

That is, if a time is in TAI, to what extent do we want to supply to the user "this is what the time is in its original timescale, TAI" and to what extent do we want to supply "this is what the time is in the timescale that everywhere else in the program (and probably your computer) uses?"

The current approach does not convert between timescale X and a "normal" timescale we are used to see, like UTC or the local time.

We just indicate that the displayed time is for example TAI, which does not mean anything, except it is **not** UTC.

I only want to achieve that we can display times with different timescale indicators. All continous timescales have a mathematical relation to UTC (which may changes over time), so we can:
1. express/display the time in a human-readable format (indicating that its not UTC but something else)
2. calculate the corresponding UTC (eventhough we don't do it - this doesn't even make sense sometimes)

Our problem at the moment is that we fully rely on UNIX timestamps. This is a hard starting-point at 1970 with a defined length of day (which does neither reflect UTC nor real-word). But we can live with that.

It depends on the protocol or the dissector to set the correct nstime. NTPv5 for example will present a TAI timestamp which is 37 seconds ahead of UTC. This will reflect a time 37 seconds ahead of an actual capture timestamp - which is fine (and correct IMO).

Others will present simple counters for seconds, weeks or whatever (looking over to GPS or Galileo). There it depends on the dissector to build an appropriate UNIX timestamp from the available information like counters + leap seconds, etc.

So, I think we can stick with the UNIX TS approach for the moment and just display timescale information instead of trying to convert times up and down.

added 1 commit
  • 26ac2248 - Proto: Implement new timescales
[Compare with previous version](/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/25913/diffs?diff_id=1923746771&start_sha=5cdb14b399cce89523a9a693cfce4c9d5edca64b)

> The current approach does not convert between timescale X and a "normal" timescale we are used to see, like UTC or the local time.

OK. Note that `ABSOLUTE_TIME_LOCAL` and `ABSOLUTE_TIME_UTC` only have to do with display. Whether a dissector uses `ABSOLUTE_TIME_LOCAL` or `ABSOLUTE_TIME_UTC` has little or nothing to do with whether a time is parsed in the packet as local time or UTC (it is parsed as UTC always; times that are local times have special handling). They only affect whether a time is displayed to a user in the local time or in UTC.

(Technically Unix time is not exactly UTC, either, even when clocks are referenced to UTC; Unix time is defined such that there are 86400 seconds in every day so that subtraction works; leap seconds are usually dealt with by repeating the last second, not really by having an extra second in the day. It's probably easier to use TAI-based Unix time.)

You're totally right - we are exactly talking about the same thing.

Conclusion:
- A dissector sets the timestamp (no matter how)
- `ABSOLUTE_TIME_*` controls what (or how) the user actually sees as representation

This is what this change is about.

> These new timescales are internally based on UNIX timestamps which represent strict 86400 SI seconds per day. Timestamps include leap seconds, which means that a timestamp pauses, repeates or jumps when leap seconds are added or deleted.

TAI just goes from 23:59:59 to 00:00:00 when UTC has a leap second, i.e. it does nothing special for leap seconds. UTC goes from 23:59:59 to 23:59:60 for a positive leap second and from 23:59:58 to 00:00:00 for a negative leap second. POSIX time does some unspecified-by-POSIX flavor of Weird **** for leap seconds to ensure that even 86401-second or 86399-second days look as if they're 86400-second days; to quote [the latest Single UNIX Specification's 4.9 "Seconds Since The Epoch"](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/basedefs/V1_chap04.html#tag_04_19), "The relationship between the actual date and time in Coordinated Universal Time, as determined by the International Earth Rotation Service, and the system's current value for seconds since the Epoch is unspecified."

So is, for example, `ABSOLUTE_TIME_TAI` represented as "the number of SI seconds that have elapsed since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC, including leap seconds"?

> Unix time is defined such that there are 86400 seconds in every day so that subtraction works

As long as "subtraction works" doesn't mean "subtracting one `time_t` value from another does not indicate the number of SI seconds that have elapsed between the two values", as it'll get the wrong answer if one or more leap seconds occurred between the two values (unless equal numbers of positive and negative leap seconds have occurred, but no negative leap seconds have ever occurred, so...).

> leap seconds are usually dealt with by repeating the last second, not really by having an extra second in the day

...or by techniques such as [leap smearing](https://developers.google.com/time/smear).

(This brings to mind [the `adjtime()` call](https://www.tuhs.org/cgi-bin/utree.pl?file=4.3BSD/usr/man/man2/adjtime.2) - it first appeared in 4.3BSD but was adopted by other Unix-like systems including SunOS 5, AIX, and Linux - which allows the system time to be changed by slowing it down or speeding it up rather than by having it make a sudden jump. It's not very usable for "you clamshelled your laptop and then opened it up again 10 days later" adjustments, but for NTP-based small tweaks it'd work. I don't know what NTP clients use it for that purpose, nor do I know whether it's used for leap smearing.)

The point is that we have to decide how to store and display times:

To give some examples:

**TAI**

Is just ticking in SI seconds. It doesn't care about the length of a day, day or night.

**UT1**

Is not ticking in SI seconds, its length is derived from astronomical observation. As long as the earth's rotation is slowing down, the UT1 second is longer than a SI second.

**UTC**

Is also ticking in SI seconds but corrected by +/- one second, determined by DUT1 (UT1-UTC) when `|DUT1| >= 0.9s`. This is the basis for a leap-second.

**GNSS Timescales (except GLONASS)**

Are continous timescales which started ticking in SI seconds, starting at a certain point in time.

**UNIX Time**

Is also a continous timescale which started ticking in SI seconds, starting at a certain point in time. With one main difference to the others: It's used to represent the UTC timescale without the actual ability to do it.

So what can we do? Currently we store times in UNIX TS which is OK when dealing with UTC times. Only exact times where leap seconds actually happend are ambigious.

We can also convert all the timescales back and forth, aslong as we know about the offset to another for a certain point in time. The IANA leap second file is already enough for this.

> As long as "subtraction works" doesn't mean "subtracting one `time_t` value from another does not [...]

What we **cannot** do is time arithmetics as long as timestamps are stored in UNIX format. When we want to store, for example a TAI time of today, we'd store it as a UNIX TS +37s. This is OK for display but not for calculations with other timestamps, because offset and/or leap information is lost.

If we need an universal solution, we'd need to store timestamps in our own SI seconds based format (also a timescale) and apply offsets and/or leap seconds when displayed. So, we could for example rely on TAI.

Note: I'm ignoring leap-smearing as it is a dynamic frequency adjustment and UT1 - both requiring data we'll not have available.

> As long as "subtraction works" doesn't mean "subtracting one time_t value from another does not indicate the number of SI seconds that have elapsed between the two values",

Correct, it gives you the number of Unix seconds, which is a SI second except on days when there's a leap second, in which case :shrug:
So which files contain time stamps in these new formats, and in which protocol's packets do time stamps in these new formats appear?

For those trying to follow along at home:  There was an attempt to move this discussion to Discord.  In discord there's a suggestion to use ML instead. See: [developer-den](https://discordapp.com/channels/889214182837321788/889214225145266288/1531252570301927646)

commits_data.message:
Proto: Implement new timescales

Added Universal Time 1 (UT1), International Atomic Time (TAI),
Terrestrial Time (TT), GPS Time (GPST), Galileo System Time (GST) and
BeiDou Time (BDT) timescales, for UT1 and TAI also with NTP variant
with all-zero-handling.

These new timescales are internally based on UNIX timestamps which
represent strict 86400 SI seconds per day. Timestamps include leap
seconds, which means that a timestamp pauses, repeates or jumps when
leap seconds are added or deleted. They are not 'visible' in the
timestamp.

The new timescales are continous timescales which means its value
constantly increases over time and is not corrected by leap seconds.

When using the timescales, it is important to know the current offset
to UTC to generate appropriate UNIX timestamps. In other use-cases
(like NTPv5 TAI) the initial offset to UTC and leap seconds are already
included in the on-wire timestamp.

The ISO 8601 representation is extended by `{ts}` scientific extensions.
This is probably the normative ISO 8601-2:2019/Amd 1:2025 notation
for this purpose.

dfilter makes use of this notation, but as it internally matches UNIX
timestamps, the timescale does not have an effect on the actual match.

Ping !25810
